titleText.es: Bueno, *yo* creo que soy real. Mírame. Mira mi cara. Si me cortas, sangro. ¿Qué más quieres? Por favor, no te vayas.
titleText.en: Well, *I* think I'm real. Look at me. Look at my face. Cut me and I'll bleed. What more do you want? Please don't go.
titleText.noteEn: The title text lets the figure in the dream argue that it is real, extending the nightmare's emotional manipulation beyond the panel.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Acostumbré is a completed-past form used by the speaker. With me before it and a after it, acostumbrarse a means to become familiar or comfortable with something through repeated experience.

example.en: I got used to the noise.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to; required after acostumbrarse before what becomes familiar
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Acostumbrarse requires a before the thing or activity that someone gets used to. Before el, a and el combine as al.

example.en: We got used to the schedule.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Here el subconsciente is used as a noun for the part of the mind outside conscious awareness.

example.es: El subconsciente influye en los sueños.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; helps form ponerse, ‘to become’
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Ponerse uses me, te, se, nos, or os to match the person or thing that enters a new state. Se is the form used with one other person or thing, or with a group that does not include the speaker or listener.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: became; got (as part of se puso + description)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Puso is the completed-past form of poner used when one other person or thing changed state. With se before it and a describing word after it, se puso presents a completed change into a new state.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: wake up (special form in a negative informal command)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Despiertes is the special tú form used after no to tell one familiar person not to wake up. Despertarse uses te with that person, so the complete command places te before the verb: no te despiertes.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: acostumbrarse a + nombre o verbo en forma de diccionario
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone gets used to a thing or activity?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a matching form of me, te, se, nos, or os with acostumbrar, then a, then the thing or activity that becomes familiar.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The small pronoun matches the person: me acostumbro, te acostumbras, se acostumbra, nos acostumbramos, or se acostumbran. Acostumbrar changes for the person and time. If an activity follows a, its verb stays in the dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The plus sign in the prompt means ‘followed by.’

example.en: We got used to the noise.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: ponerse + palabra que describe un estado
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something becomes a new state, such as nervous, pale, or dark?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a matching form of me, te, se, nos, or os with poner, followed by a word that describes the new state.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The small pronoun matches whoever changes, and poner changes for the person and time: me pongo, te pones, se puso, nos pusimos. The describing word matches that person or thing: nervioso, nerviosa, nerviosos, or nerviosas. Ponerse commonly presents a noticeable change in emotion, appearance, or condition, often one that is quick or temporary. The plus sign in the prompt means ‘followed by.’

applications.exampleEs: ME ACOSTUMBRÉ A LAS PESADILLAS NORMALES
applications.explanationEn: Me matches the speaker, acostumbré is the completed-past form, a introduces what became familiar, and las pesadillas normales fills that complement.
Acostumbré presents the transition into familiarity as a completed past event rather than as continuing background.
Pesadillas names the things first, and normales follows it with the neutral description.
Pesadillas is plural, so normales uses its plural form ending in -es; normal has the same form for masculine and feminine nouns.
Se matches mi subconsciente, the thing that changes; puso presents the completed change, and creativo names the resulting masculine-singular state.
Puso presents the change into a new state as a completed past event rather than as an ongoing background condition.

regions.labelEs: POR FAVOR, NO TE DESPIERTES. NO QUIERO MORIR.

applications.explanationEn: Por and favor work together as the fixed politeness expression.
No starts the negative instruction, te matches the familiar listener in despertarse, and despiertes is the special negative-command form.
Quiero changes for the speaker, while morir stays in its unchanged dictionary form as the desired action.
